title: Tube-feeding a newborn lamb
subtitle: Getting colostrum into a weak or hypothermic lamb using a stomach tube.
excerpt: A newborn lamb that is too weak to suckle within the first two hours of life faces a rapidly closing window for passive immunity transfer from colostrum. Stomach tubing is the reliable alternative to a bottle when a lamb lacks the strength or suckling reflex to feed. The technique is straightforward once learned and is one of the most valuable skills in a lambing shed. Every lamber should know it before the lambing season starts.
sourceNotes: AHDB Beef and Lamb, Better Returns Programme: Sheep BRP Manual 1: Colostrum Management (2022). Moredun Research Institute, Neonatal lamb care and hypothermia (2021). DEFRA Code of Recommendations for the Welfare of Sheep (2018). SAC Consulting, Lamb Tube Feeding Training Guide (2020).

glossaryTerms.definition: The first milk produced by a ewe after lambing, rich in immunoglobulins that provide the lamb with passive immunity for the first weeks of life. Absorption from the gut drops sharply after six hours and is negligible after 24 hours.
A flexible plastic tube, typically 40 to 50 cm long, passed through the lamb's mouth and down into the stomach to deliver colostrum or milk directly when the suckling reflex is absent or too weak.

Immunity transferred from the ewe to the lamb via colostrum immunoglobulins absorbed through the gut wall. The window for absorption is open from birth but closes rapidly: by 24 hours the gut is no longer permeable to immunoglobulins.

content.text: A lamb born weak, chilled, or from a difficult birth may lack the strength to suckle. Bottle-feeding relies on a suckling reflex; if the reflex is absent, the milk pools in the mouth and risks entering the airway. A
stomach tube
bypasses the reflex entirely and gets
colostrum
directly into the stomach, where it is safe and begins digesting immediately.
The window for colostrum absorption providing
passive immunity
closes fast. Aim to get the first tube feed into a weak lamb within the first two hours of life. A lamb that has been waiting for an hour while you try a bottle has already lost some of that window.
What you need
A lamb stomach tube and reservoir bag, clean and sterilised. A standard lamb tube kit has a soft flexible tube (usually red or yellow) attached to a 250 ml reservoir bag with a clip.
Fresh ewe colostrum milked from the dam, or frozen colostrum from your colostrum bank, thawed to 38 degrees Celsius in a water bath. Never microwave colostrum; it destroys immunoglobulins.
A thermometer to confirm colostrum temperature.
Dose

The standard guidance is 50 ml of colostrum per kilogram of lamb body weight, given as the first feed. A 3.5 kg lamb receives 175 ml. The stomach of a newborn lamb holds around 200 to 250 ml comfortably. Do not overfill: a bloated stomach can inhibit breathing in a weak lamb.
Procedure
Sit with the lamb upright on your knee, facing away from you, body between your knees. The head should be held in a neutral position, not extended back.
Measure the tube length before passing it: lay the tube alongside the lamb from its mouth to its last rib. The stomach is roughly at the last rib. Mark that point on the tube with your thumb.

Gently open the lamb's mouth and slide the tube over the tongue and into the back of the throat. A swallowing movement helps the tube pass into the oesophagus rather than the trachea. Advance slowly to your measured mark.

Confirm placement: blow gently into the tube while a second person places a hand on the lamb's left flank. You should feel or hear the air in the rumen. If the lamb coughs or shows respiratory distress, withdraw the tube immediately.

Once confirmed in the stomach, clip the reservoir bag to your clothing at shoulder height and allow the colostrum to flow in by gravity. Do not squeeze the bag: gravity flow is slow enough to be safe. Let the correct dose flow in over two to three minutes.
Pinch the tube closed, withdraw it smoothly, and return the lamb to a warm environment with the ewe.
After tube feeding
Keep the lamb warm. A cold lamb may struggle to absorb and digest until its core temperature recovers to 38 to 39 degrees.
Check for suckling reflex 30 to 60 minutes after tube feeding. As core temperature rises, many lambs recover sufficient strength to suckle independently.
Tube feed again every four hours if the suckling reflex remains absent.

attrs.cue: Lamb coughs when tube is passed
attrs.cause: Tube has entered the trachea rather than the oesophagus
attrs.fix: Withdraw the tube immediately. Allow the lamb to recover for a minute, then retry with the head in a more neutral position. Accidental tracheal administration of colostrum can cause aspiration pneumonia or rapid death.

attrs.cue: Colostrum does not flow from the bag
attrs.cause: Bag held too low, tube kinked, or clip not released
attrs.fix: Check the clip is open. Hold the bag above shoulder height. Check the tube for kinks and straighten. Do not squeeze the bag.
